name: Amraphel
title: King of Shinar
summary: Amrafel was king of Shinar, the biblical name for Babylonia, and one of four allied kings who, under Kedorlaomer's leadership, carried out a major military campaign in the Canaan region. The coalition defeated several peoples in Transjordan before overcoming five rebellious vassal kings in the Valley of Siddim and plundering Sodom and Gomorrah. During the plundering, Lot, Abraham's nephew, was taken captive. This prompted Abraham's bold counterattack with 318 men, which resulted in Lot's rescue and then the remarkable meeting with Melchizedek, priest and king of Salem. Amrafel appears only in Genesis 14, a chapter that is unique among the patriarchal narratives for placing Abraham in an international, military-political context, thereby highlighting his role as a powerful leader, not merely a nomadic shepherd.

keyEvents.title: The Coalition of Four Kings
keyEvents.description: Amraphel was part of a military coalition together with Chedorlaomer, king of Elam, Tidal, king of Goiim, and Arioch, king of Ellasar. Chedorlaomer was the leading king, since it was his dominion that the vassal kings in the Valley of Siddim had rebelled against.

keyEvents.title: The War Against the Five Kings in the Valley of Siddim
keyEvents.description: The four allied kings, including Amraphel, went to war against five kings: Bera of Sodom, Birsha of Gomorrah, Shinab of Admah, Shemeber of Zeboiim, and the king of Bela (Zoar).

keyEvents.title: The Campaign Through Transjordan
keyEvents.description: On their way to the Valley of Siddim, the coalition defeated several peoples, including the Rephaim, the Zuzim, the Emim, and the Horites, in an extensive military campaign through Transjordan.

keyEvents.title: Victory in the Valley of Siddim
keyEvents.description: Amraphel and his allies defeated the five kings in the Valley of Siddim, which was full of tar pits. The kings of Sodom and Gomorrah fell into the pits while fleeing, while the rest escaped to the mountains. However, the king of Sodom survived and met Abraham after the victory.

keyEvents.title: The Plundering of Sodom and Gomorrah
keyEvents.description: After their victory, the four kings plundered Sodom and Gomorrah, taking all possessions and food supplies, as well as Lot, Abraham's nephew, and his belongings.

keyEvents.title: Abraham's Counterattack and Rescue of Lot
keyEvents.description: When Abraham heard that Lot had been taken captive, he mustered 318 trained men from his household, pursued the coalition all the way to Dan and further to Hobah north of Damascus, defeated them, and rescued Lot along with all his possessions. This marked the end of Amraphel's campaign.

versions.summary: Amraphel was the king of Shinar (Babylonia) who allied himself with three other kings in a campaign against five kings in the Valley of Siddim. This military campaign led to Lot, Abraham's nephew, being taken captive, which triggered Abraham's rescue operation. Amraphel is mentioned only in Genesis 14 and is known as one of the first kings mentioned in the Bible.
versions.title: King of Shinar
versions.reason: [minor] The title 'King of Shinar' is correct but could be more descriptive to contextualize his role in the biblical narrative.; [minor] The phrasing 'one of the first kings mentioned in the Bible' is somewhat imprecise. There are kings mentioned earlier in Genesis (for example, Nimrod is described as a mighty ruler in Gen 10:8-12). It could be clarified to 'one of the first foreign kings mentioned in the patriarchal narratives'.; [minor] The role 'warrior' is acceptable, but 'military ally' or 'leader of an alliance' might be more precise. Amraphel is primarily known as a king who participated in a military coalition, not as an individual warrior. However, we retain 'warrior' as it is sufficiently descriptive.; [minor] In the event 'Alliance of Four Kings', it states that Amraphel 'formed' the alliance, but the text in Gen 14 rather indicates that Chedorlaomer was the leading king in the coalition (see vv. 4-5 where the vassal kings rebel against Chedorlaomer). Amraphel's role as initiator should be downplayed.; [minor] In 'The Victory in the Valley of Siddim', it states that the kings of Sodom and Gomorrah 'fled and fell there'. The Hebrew text in Gen 14:10 can be interpreted to mean they fell into the tar pits, but the king of Sodom appears again in v. 17, suggesting he survived. The phrasing should be clarified.; [minor] In the event 'Abraham's Counterattack and Defeat', the title is somewhat ambiguous – 'defeat' could mistakenly be read as Abraham's defeat. A clearer title would have been 'Abraham's Counterattack and Rescue of Lot'.; [major] Footnotes are missing. Amraphel is a figure with rich historical and linguistic discussion, including the earlier (now rejected) identification with Hammurabi, and relevant footnotes should be added.

The coalition carried out an extensive campaign against five rebellious vassal kings in the Valley of Siddim. During the plundering of Sodom and Gomorrah, Lot, Abraham's nephew, was taken captive, which triggered Abraham's bold rescue operation with 318 men. Amraphel is mentioned only in Genesis 14 and is one of the first foreign kings to appear in the patriarchal narratives.

versions.reason: [minor] The description states that "the kings of Sodom and Gomorrah fell while fleeing into the pits, but the king of Sodom clearly survived (cf. v. 17)." This is somewhat confusingly worded. The text in Gen 14:10 says that the kings of Sodom and Gomorrah fell into the tar pits, yet the king of Sodom appears again in v. 17. The wording should be clarified.; [minor] The summary is good but closely resembles the previous version. It could be enriched with more theological perspective, for example, Amraphel's role as a contrast to Abraham's faith and the following Melchizedek episode.; [minor] A footnote about the rabbinic tradition surrounding Amraphel could enrich the profile. In the Talmud (Eruvin 53a), the rabbis identify Amraphel with Nimrod, based on a wordplay where "Amraphel" is interpreted as "he who commanded (amar) to cast (hipil) Abraham into the fiery furnace."

footnotes.text: Amraphel was formerly often identified with Hammurabi of Babylon, but this identification has now largely been abandoned by scholars. The linguistic and chronological arguments do not hold, and the names have different etymologies.

Shinar is the biblical name for southern Mesopotamia, roughly corresponding to Babylonia. The name appears several times in the Old Testament (Gen 10:10; 11:2; Isa 11:11; Dan 1:2) and refers to the plain between the Euphrates and Tigris.

Genesis 14 is unique among the patriarchal narratives because it places Abraham in an international military context. The chapter has a distinct literary style that differs from the rest of Genesis, and some scholars believe it is based on a very ancient source.

Kedorlaomer of Elam appears to have been the actual leader of the coalition, since it is against his overlordship that the vassal kings revolt (Gen 14:4). Amraphel is mentioned first in the list, which may reflect a geographical or literary arrangement rather than rank.

The Valley of Siddim, where the battle took place, is traditionally identified with the area south of the Dead Sea. The 'slime pits' (Hebrew: be'erot hemar) mentioned in Gen 14:10 refer to natural asphalt or bitumen pits typical of this region.

In rabbinic tradition (Talmud, Eruvin 53a), Amraphel is identified with Nimrod. The name 'Amraphel' is interpreted through a wordplay as 'he who commanded (amar) to cast down (hipil)' – a reference to the tradition that Nimrod threw Abraham into a fiery furnace. This identification has no support in modern scholarship but testifies to the Jewish exegetical tradition surrounding this figure.
